title: Explain the ‘Four-Part Test’ for R&D tax credits in simple terms
description: The four-part test for the federal R&D credit under IRC section 41: permitted purpose, technological uncertainty, hard science, experimentation.
summary: The R&D tax credit four-part test, explained: under IRC section 41, U.S. businesses can claim the federal research credit only for qualified research that meets every requirement—a permitted purpose of improving function, performance, reliability, or quality; technological uncertainty at the outset; reliance on hard science; and a process of experimentation—applied separately to each business component.

body.text: The R&D tax credit four-part test, explained: under IRC section 41, U.S. businesses can claim the federal research credit only for qualified research that meets every requirement—a permitted purpose of improving function, performance, reliability, or quality; technological uncertainty at the outset; reliance on hard science; and a process of experimentation—applied separately to each business component.
This report is general information, not tax or legal advice.
1. The short version

The federal research credit lives in Internal Revenue Code section 41, titled “Credit for increasing research activities.” A business can only count costs toward the credit if they were spent on qualified research, and research is only “qualified” if it passes four tests at the same time. Fail any one test and the activity, and the costs tied to it, do not count toward the credit. The costs that do count are called qualified research expenses, or QREs.
In plain words, the four questions are:

items: Purpose: Were you trying to make a product, process, or piece of software work better—that is, improve its function, performance, reliability, or quality?
Uncertainty: At the start, did you genuinely not know whether you could do it, how to do it, or what the right design was?
Technological in nature: Did the work rely on hard science—the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science?
Process of experimentation: Did you work through the problem methodically, identifying alternatives, testing them, and evaluating the results?

body.text: The statute and the IRS group the same ideas slightly differently, and one of the official four tests (the section 174A test) does not appear in the popular version at all. Section 2 explains how the two versions line up.

A useful way to remember the whole test: the law wants to reward businesses that face a real technical unknown, attack it with real science, and do so in a disciplined, trial-and-error way, all for the sake of making something work better. It does not reward routine work, cosmetic changes, or business research that happens to involve a product.
2. Where the test comes from
The governing law frames it this way:

items: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), research qualifies only if (A) it is research with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A; (B) it is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature and the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer; and (C) substantially all of its activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in § 41(d)(3). Activities listed in § 41(d)(4) are excluded no matter what.

The IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, for the January 2025 revision of the form) restate these as four requirements: (1) the expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A (the “section 174A test”); (2) the research is undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature (the “technological information test”); (3) the application of the research is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component (the “business component test”); and (4) substantially all of the research activities are elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (the “process of experimentation test”).

body.text: Correction 1 (currency of the statute): The first statutory requirement now refers to section 174A. Pub. L. 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025) amended § 41(d)(1)(A) generally. The prior text referred to research “with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174.” The current text refers to research “with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A.” The popular four-label version does not mention this element at all. In simple terms, this requirement means the costs must first be the kind of research costs the tax code recognizes for domestic research or experimental expenditures before the credit rules can even be applied.

Correction 2 (sequencing): The law does not require the tests to be run in a fixed order. What it requires is that all of them are met, and that they are applied separately to each business component. Section 41(d)(2)(A) states that paragraph (1) “shall be applied separately with respect to each business component of the taxpayer,” and the Form 6765 instructions repeat that the test must be applied separately to each business component. Many practitioners do walk through the tests in a set order as a practical checklist, which is a reasonable working habit but not a legal requirement.

Analysis: The two framings cover the same ground. The “uncertainty” idea comes from the section 174 definition of research in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and is built into the credit regulations both in the discussion of discovering technological information (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)) and in the definition of a process of experimentation, which applies where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)). The “permitted purpose” idea is the qualified-purpose rule in § 41(d)(3), combined with the business-component requirement in § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(B). The four-label version is a teaching tool; the statute and regulations carry the legal weight.

Correction 3 (citation precision): That paragraph does speak of uncertainty “at the outset” in defining a process of experimentation, but the regulation’s main statement of the uncertainty requirement for the credit is in § 1.41-4(a)(3). Both citations are now given.
3. The four parts, one at a time
3.1 Permitted purpose: making something better

What the law says. Research is treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to (i) a new or improved function, (ii) performance, or (iii) reliability or quality (§ 41(d)(3)(A)). Research shall in no event be treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors (§ 41(d)(3)(B)). The credit regulations repeat this purpose requirement as part of the process-of-experimentation rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)).

What is a “business component”? Any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be (i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer (§ 41(d)(2)(B)). This condition matters because research that never connects to something the business sells, licenses, leases, or uses in its operations does not have a business component to attach to.

In simple terms: the goal must be a technical improvement, not a new look. Developing a lighter, stronger material for a car chassis points toward a permitted purpose; repainting the chassis a new color for the model year does not. The second matches the statutory exclusion for cosmetic and seasonal design factors. A product can be “new” to the taxpayer and still qualify; the statute speaks of a “new or improved” business component, so the improvement need not be new to the world.

Recommended documentation (consistent with IRS guidance that records should be contemporaneous): project charters, product roadmaps, and scope documents that state the specific technical objective from the outset, together with time records tied to the project. A bare statement such as “we built a new system” does not show what was being improved or how. A stronger statement identifies the measurable target, for example a required load capacity, processing speed, failure rate, or tolerance, and explains why meeting it was a functional, performance, reliability, or quality goal rather than an aesthetic one.
3.2 Elimination of uncertainty: you didn’t know the answer at the start

What the law says. Under the section 174 regulations, activities are research or experimental if they are intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)). The credit regulations apply the same idea to business components: research must be undertaken to discover technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty about the development or improvement of a business component, and uncertainty exists if the information available does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or its appropriate design (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)). The process-of-experimentation rule likewise applies where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain as of the outset (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)).

In simple terms: three questions—Can we do it? How do we do it? What should it look like (in an engineering, not cosmetic, sense)? If the answers to all three were already known from standard practice or readily available information, there is nothing uncertain to resolve.

Two clarifications from the regulations. First, the credit regulation states that a taxpayer does not have to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field; the question is whether the information available to the taxpayer established the answer, not whether the research advanced the state of the art for the whole industry (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)). Second, the regulation provides that the issuance of a U.S. utility patent is conclusive evidence that the taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature and intended to eliminate uncertainty, though a patent is not required to qualify (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)). The patent rule speaks only to the discovery-of-information element; the other requirements, including the process-of-experimentation test, still apply.

Success is not required. The section 174 regulation confirms that the ultimate success, failure, sale, or use of the product is not relevant to a determination of eligibility under section 174 (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)), and the credit regulation likewise does not require the taxpayer to succeed in developing a new or improved business component (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)). The costs still have to meet every other requirement of the test and the expense rules of § 41(b).

Recommended documentation: feasibility studies, early engineering logs, risk assessments, and proposals that name the technical unknowns at the start of the project. The best records are dated and show what the team did not know before work began, rather than describing the uncertainty only after the outcome was known.
3.3 Technological in nature: grounded in hard science

What the law says. Information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)). The regulation adds that a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and may rely on existing principles of those sciences to satisfy this requirement. Research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities is excluded (§ 41(d)(4)(G)), as are efficiency surveys, activities relating to management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collection, and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control (§ 41(d)(4)(D)).
Correction 4 (wording): Chemistry is not listed separately in the regulation; it falls within the physical sciences. The practical meaning is the same.

Quality control vs. design testing. Ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control is excluded from research or experimental expenditures (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)), but the regulation clarifies that quality control testing does not include testing to determine if the design of the product is appropriate (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7)). In simple terms, checking that a finished widget meets a known specification is routine; testing whether the widget’s design will hold up at all is part of research.

In simple terms: writing code to make a database query algorithm faster relies on computer science; surveying customers about whether they want a faster database is market research (consistent with § 41(d)(4)(D)). That is a fair reading, since the rule looks at the scientific principles relied on, not the credentials of the people involved, and the regulation expressly allows reliance on existing technologies and principles. No credential requirement appears in § 41 or § 1.41-4.

Recommended documentation: design specifications and technical manuals showing which scientific or engineering principles were used, and records showing that the people whose wages are claimed had the technical background to perform, directly supervise, or directly support the work.
3.4 Process of experimentation: methodical trial and evaluation

What the law says. A process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer’s research activities. It involves identifying the uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate it, and conducting a process of evaluating the alternatives, for example through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology. It must be an evaluative process and generally should be capable of evaluating more than one alternative. It must also relate to a qualified purpose—a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality—and not to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)).

The “substantially all” rule. The statute requires that substantially all of the activities be elements of a process of experimentation (§ 41(d)(1)(C)). The regulation sets this at 80 percent or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, applied separately to each business component (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)).

Clarification. The regulation also explains that if 80 percent or more of the activities are elements of a process of experimentation, the remaining 20 percent or less do not themselves have to be experimentation, but they must still satisfy the section 174A and technological-information requirements and must not fall within any of the § 41(d)(4) exclusions (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)). In simple terms, the small share of non-experimental work can ride along with the qualifying research, but only if it is genuinely part of that research and not an excluded activity such as market research.

Worked example (hypothetical). A company spends $200,000 on activities for one new valve design. Of that, $170,000 goes to building prototypes, running pressure tests on three alternative seal materials, and analyzing the results; $30,000 goes to related work that is not experimentation. Step 1: $170,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.85. Step 2: 0.85 = 85%. Step 3: 85% is at least 80%, so the substantially-all requirement is met for this business component (the other requirements must still be satisfied, and the $30,000 must itself meet the section 174A and technological-information requirements and not be excluded). If only $150,000 had been experimentation, the share would be $150,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.75, or 75%, which falls short at the whole-component level.

The shrinking-back rule (analysis). When a whole business component fails, the regulations provide that the test is next applied to the most significant subset of elements of that component, and then to the next most significant subset, until a qualifying subset is found or the most basic element fails (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)). In the 75% example above, this means a smaller subset of the valve project, such as the seal subsystem, might still qualify on its own even though the whole valve design does not. This rule is noted here because it directly governs how the substantially-all test is applied in practice; the taxpayer still needs records detailed enough to identify the subset.
In simple terms: form a hypothesis, test it, look at the results, adjust, and test again—and keep records of each round, including failures.

Recommended documentation: records of the hypothesis and planned method; lab notes, test protocols, drawings, simulation screenshots, and prototype photos showing test conditions and variables; and meeting notes, emails, and reports showing how results (successes and failures) led to changes in the next iteration.
4. Activities that never qualify, even if they seem technical
Section 41(d)(4) lists exclusions that apply regardless of the four parts, and § 41(d)(3)(B) separately removes cosmetic and seasonal work from the permitted purpose.

cells: Changes to style, taste, or appearance only

Efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collection, routine or ordinary quality-control testing or inspection
Software developed primarily for the taxpayer’s own internal use, except as provided in regulations (see below)
Research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or a governmental entity

body.text: Internal-use software. Section 41(d)(4)(E) excludes, except to the extent provided in regulations, research with respect to computer software developed by or for the benefit of the taxpayer primarily for internal use, other than software used in an activity that constitutes qualified research or in a production process that meets the qualified-research requirements. The regulations provide that internal-use software can still qualify if, in addition to the general four-part test, it satisfies the “high threshold of innovation” test in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii), which has three requirements:

items: Innovative: the software would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful.

Significant economic risk: the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development, and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period.

Not commercially available: the software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for its intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the innovative and significant-economic-risk requirements.

body.text: In simple terms, building an ordinary in-house tool—even with real programming—usually will not qualify unless the project was a genuine, risky leap that could not be bought off the shelf. The regulation also contains separate rules for dual-function software (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)).
5. Linking the four parts to records

Passing the test is not enough—you must be able to show it. The IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (LMSB-04-0508-030, dated May 2008; IRS web page last reviewed or updated July 2, 2026) says supporting information should be contemporaneous and available for inspection, states that taxpayers are required to maintain records that enable them to delineate accurately the amounts expended for research, notes that the IRS is not required to accept estimates or extrapolations because taxpayers must keep records under section 6001, and instructs examiners that arbitrary and unsupported allocations should not be accepted. The guide itself cautions that its technical accuracy is not guaranteed after its publication date, so it should be read alongside the current statute, regulations, and form instructions.

Correction 5 (estimates): The IRS guide is stricter in tone: it tells examiners that arbitrary and unsupported allocations should not be accepted, that allocation percentages may be accepted only when the prerequisites for that approach are met, and that a claim relying too heavily on high-level estimations may warrant disallowance or return to the taxpayer for perfection. Estimates drawn from interviews or judgment sampling are not treated as sufficient substantiation on their own. Treat estimates with caution and back them with documents created at the time the work was done.

cells: The specific functional, performance, reliability, or quality improvement sought for a business component held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the business
Project charters, roadmaps, scope documents; time sheets tied to the project
What was unknown about capability, method, or appropriate design at the start
Feasibility studies, early engineering logs, risk assessments
Reliance on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science
Design specifications, technical manuals, staff qualifications
Alternatives identified and evaluated, results analyzed, design adjusted; 80% substantially-all threshold met per business component
Test reports, prototype revisions, emails on design failures, project logs

body.text: 5.1 Reporting by business component on Form 6765

Under the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, for the January 2025 revision of the form), Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025, unless an exception applies. When Section G is required, filers must report at least 80% of total qualified research expenses by business component, using no more than 50 business components (the “80%/Top 50” approach), listed in descending order by QREs, with any remaining components reported in aggregate. Wages are broken out into those for conducting, directly supervising, and directly supporting the research, alongside supplies, computer rental or lease costs, and contract research.

Two exceptions exist. Section G is not required for (1) a qualified small business under § 41(h)(3) that checks the box to elect the reduced payroll tax credit, or (2) a filer for whom all three of the following apply: total QREs at the controlled-group level are $1.5 million or less; average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less; and the credit is reported on an original return.

Analysis: because the four-part test is applied component by component under § 41(d)(2)(A), this reporting format mirrors how the test itself works. A taxpayer that already organizes its four-part documentation by business component, as Section 5 recommends, will find Section G far easier to complete.
6. Scope note

Expense rules under § 41(b), such as the exclusion of land and depreciable property from supplies (§ 41(b)(2)(C)), are mentioned only in passing because they govern which costs count, not whether an activity passes the four-part test.
